topic.name: Stroke & TIA
objectives: Know tPA window, eligibility, and contraindications
Understand TIA workup (ABCD² score, urgent evaluation)
Implement secondary prevention strategies (antiplatelets, statins, BP control)

content_chunks.title: Why This Matters
content_chunks.content: Meet James: 64, hypertensive, smoker. He was eating lunch when suddenly his right arm went numb and he couldn't speak. His wife called 911. In the ED, a CT shows no bleed. He's within the tPA window — but the clock is ticking. Every minute without treatment, 1.9 million neurons die. Stroke is the #5 cause of death and #1 cause of long-term disability in the US. 795,000 strokes occur yearly — that's one every 40 seconds. As an FNP, YOU are often the first to evaluate — your recognition speed determines outcomes.
content_chunks.visual_desc: Brain clock: Normal brain hemisphere vs. ischemic hemisphere showing the 'time is brain' concept with 1.9M neurons lost per minute, with FAST acronym overlaid

content_chunks.title: What IS a Stroke?
content_chunks.content:
**Stroke**: Rapidly developing focal neurologic deficit from **vascular cause** lasting >24 hours (or with infarction on imaging).

**TIA** (Transient Ischemic Attack): Same symptoms but resolve in <24 hours (usually <1 hour) with NO infarction on imaging.

**Two Main Types**:

**ISCHEMIC STROKE** (87% of all strokes)
• Blockage of blood vessel by clot
• **Thrombotic**: Clot forms locally on atherosclerotic plaque
• **Embolic**: Clot travels from elsewhere (carotid, heart — think AFib!)
• **Lacunar**: Small vessel disease (HTN, DM — small deep infarcts)

**HEMORRHAGIC STROKE** (13% of strokes, but 40% of deaths)
• Blood vessel ruptures
• **Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH)**: HTN most common cause
• **Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH)**: from aneurysm rupture — 'worst headache of my life'

**Key point**: YOU CAN'T tell ischemic vs. hemorrhagic clinically — need CT scan! tPA given to hemorrhagic = disaster!
content_chunks.visual_desc: Side-by-side brain slices: LEFT (ischemic): dark area of infarction. RIGHT (hemorrhagic): bright white blood in brain tissue

content_chunks.title: FAST: The Stroke Recognition Tool
content_chunks.content:
**FAST** (the gold standard for public + providers):

**F — Face**: Ask them to smile. Is one side drooping? (facial asymmetry)

**A — Arms**: Ask them to raise both arms. Does one drift down? (arm drift)

**S — Speech**: Ask them to say a full sentence ('You can't teach an old dog new tricks'). Is it slurred? Garbled? Word-finding? (aphasia/dysarthria)

**T — Time**: Time of **LAST KNOWN WELL** = when they were last seen normal — this determines tPA eligibility! Don't ask 'when did symptoms start' — ask 'when were they last seen normal?'

**BEFAST** (expanded version):
**B** — Balance (sudden dizziness, loss of coordination)
**E** — Eyes (sudden vision loss, double vision, visual field cut)
**F, A, S, T** as above

**Stroke Mimics** (things that look like stroke but aren't):
• Hypoglycemia (always check fingerstick!)
• Seizure with post-ictal paralysis (Todd paralysis)
• Migraine with aura
• Bell's palsy (peripheral vs. central face — forehead spared in stroke)
• Conversion disorder
• Electrolyte abnormalities
content_chunks.clinical_pearl: 🔥 **Always check fingerstick glucose FIRST!** Severe hypoglycemia (glucose <50) can exactly mimic stroke symptoms. Treating hypoglycemia as 'stroke' with tPA would be catastrophic — and it's such an easy fix!

quick_checks.q: What percentage of strokes are ischemic?
quick_checks.explanation: **87%** of strokes are ischemic (blockage). 13% are hemorrhagic (bleed). But hemorrhagic causes 40% of stroke deaths!

quick_checks.q: A patient with sudden right-sided weakness and aphasia arrives 3 hours after last seen normal. Fingerstick glucose = 92. Best first step?
quick_checks.explanation: **Stat non-contrast CT head** is the VERY FIRST step after ABCs and fingerstick. Must rule out hemorrhage before any anticoagulation or tPA!

content_chunks.title: The Golden Hour
content_chunks.content: Maria arrives at the ED. CT shows no hemorrhage. She's 72, hypertensive, and was last normal at 4 PM — it's now 6:30 PM (symptoms started ~2.5 hours ago). She's a tPA candidate! But wait — she had knee replacement surgery 10 days ago. Does that preclude tPA? What about her BP of 195/110? The clock keeps ticking. Every decision you make — or delay — costs brain cells. This is stroke code. This is high-stakes medicine.
content_chunks.visual_desc: Decision tree: Stroke patient → CT non-contrast → No bleed → Check tPA eligibility (time, BP, anticoag, recent surgery) → Eligible → tPA infusion

content_chunks.title: tPA (Alteplase) Protocol: The 3-Hour Window
content_chunks.content:
**tPA Eligibility Criteria** (must meet ALL):

✅ **Age ≥18** (no upper age limit!)
✅ **Time**: Last known normal <3 hours (can extend to 4.5 hours in some cases)
✅ **CT**: No intracranial hemorrhage on non-contrast CT
✅ **NIH Stroke Scale**: Measurable neurologic deficit

**tPA EXCLUSIONS (Know These Cold!)**

**Absolute Contraindications** (DO NOT GIVE):
🔴 ICH on CT (any bleed!)
🔴 Acute intracranial hemorrhage history
🔴 **BP >185/110** despite treatment (must lower BP first!)
🔴 Active internal bleeding (GI, GU bleed within 21 days)
🔴 Recent **major surgery** (<14 days) or **head trauma** (<3 months)
🔴 **Intracranial surgery** (<3 months)
🔴 **INR >1.7** or PT >15 sec
🔴 **Platelets <100,000**
🔴 **Glucose <50 or >400** (treat hypoglycemia first!)
🔴 Known bleeding diathesis
🔴 Recent lumbar puncture (<7 days)

**Relative Contraindications** (weigh risk/benefit):
⚠️ **Age >80** (for 3-4.5 hour window)
⚠️ **NIHSS >25** (massive stroke = higher bleed risk)
⚠️ **Seizure** at onset
⚠️ **Recent MI** (<3 months)
⚠️ **Pregnancy**
⚠️ **Rapidly improving symptoms** (but don't wait too long!)

**Dosing**: 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg)
• 10% as bolus over 1 minute
• Remaining 90% over 60 minutes

**Post-tPA Monitoring**:
• **BP <180/105** for 24 hours
• Neuro checks q15min × 2 hours, then q30min × 6 hours, then hourly
• No aspirin, heparin, or anticoag for 24 hours
• Hold all needles/NG tubes/arterial lines
• Stat CT if: worsening neuro status, severe headache, vomiting, BP surge
content_chunks.mnemonic: **tPA NO = BATH BAGS**: **B**P >185/110, **A**nticoagulated (INR >1.7), **T**rauma/surgery <14d, **H**emorrhage on CT, **B**leeding active, **A**ge >80 (relative), **G**lucose <50/>400, **S**eizure at onset
content_chunks.visual_desc: Color-coded checklist: GREEN box (eligible criteria) on left, RED box (absolute contraindications) with skull-and-crossbones icons, YELLOW box (relative contraindications) with caution icons

content_chunks.title: Hemorrhagic Stroke: The Other Side
content_chunks.content:
**Intracerebral Hemorrhage (ICH)** — know the differences from ischemic!

**Presentation**:
• **Severe headache** (most common symptom)
• Nausea/vomiting (more common than ischemic)
• **Decreased consciousness** (worse than ischemic)
• Rapid deterioration
• Hypertension (extremely high BP)

**Causes**:
• **Hypertension** (most common — causes small vessel rupture)
• Anticoagulation (warfarin, DOACs — MUCH worse outcomes)
• Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (elderly)
• AV malformations, aneurysms
• Trauma
• Cocaine/amphetamines (severe HTN spike)

**Management**:
1. **STOP anticoagulation** (reverse!):
   • Warfarin: **Vitamin K** IV + **PCC** (4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate) or FFP
   • DOACs: **Andexanet alfa** (for apixaban/rivarelbant), **idarucizumab** (for dabigatran)
2. **BP control**: SBP <140 (intensive lowering improves outcomes)
3. **Neurosurgery consult**: for posterior fossa bleeds, large lobar bleeds, or if herniating
4. **Seizure prophylaxis**: Avoid (no benefit) — but treat if seizures occur
5. **Intracranial pressure monitoring**: if GCS ≤8

**Worse prognosis with**: Age >80, ICH volume >30 mL, infratentorial location, intraventricular extension, anticoagulation use
content_chunks.clinical_pearl: 🔥 **Warfarin-related ICH is the WORST** — risk of hematoma expansion is HIGH. Give **Vitamin K 10 mg IV + PCC** stat. PCC works faster than FFP (minutes vs. hours needed to thaw and infuse!). Don't wait for INR to normalize — give PCC immediately!

content_chunks.content: 🔥 **'Wake-up' strokes** — patient goes to bed normal, wakes with deficits. Time of last known well = bedtime. Most wake-up strokes are NOT tPA-eligible unless advanced imaging (MRI DWI/perfusion mismatch) shows salvageable tissue. Some centers use CT perfusion to extend window up to 24 hours — but this is specialized.

mnemonics.mnemonic: **tPA NO = BATH BAGS**: **B**P >185/110, **A**nticoagulated (INR >1.7), **T**rauma/surgery <14d, **H**emorrhage on CT, **B**leeding active, **A**ge >80 (relative), **G**lucose <50/>400, **S**eizure at onset

quick_checks.q: Patient with ischemic stroke 2 hours ago, BP 200/110. Can you give tPA?
a: No, must lower BP to <185/110 first, then reassess
No, BP is never a contraindication
quick_checks.explanation: BP must be **<185/110** before tPA. Give IV labetalol or nicardipine to lower. Once controlled, can give tPA. But if BP remains refractory, tPA is contraindicated.

quick_checks.q: Which is a contraindication to tPA regardless of time window?
quick_checks.explanation: **INR >1.7** is an absolute contraindication (increased bleeding risk). Age >80 is only a relative contraindication (for 3-4.5 hr window). NIHSS 10 is treatable. AFib is an indication, not contraindication!

lessons.title: ⚠️ TIA & Secondary Prevention: Don't Miss the Warning Shot

content_chunks.title: The Warning Shot
content_chunks.content: Meet Fred: 67, diabetic, hypertensive. Last week his left arm went numb and he couldn't see out of his left eye for 10 minutes. Then it resolved completely. He didn't go to the ER because 'it went away.' He's telling you about it today at his annual physical. This is a classic **TIA** — specifically **amaurosis fugax** (transient monocular vision loss from carotid emboli). His risk of stroke in the next 90 days is 10-20% without treatment. This is your chance to prevent a catastrophic stroke.
content_chunks.visual_desc: Timeline: TIA (symptoms resolve <24h) → High-risk period → 10-20% stroke risk in 90 days → Preventive treatment blocks progression to full stroke

content_chunks.title: TIA: What It Is & Why It Matters
content_chunks.content:
**TIA** (Transient Ischemic Attack): Temporary episode of neurologic dysfunction caused by **focal brain ischemia** without infarction.

**Key Features**:
• Symptoms resolve **completely** (usually within 5-60 minutes)
• **By definition** <24 hours (most <1 hour)
• No stroke on **MRI DWI** (if DWI shows infarction = stroke, not TIA!)

**HIGH-YEAR: Symptoms by Vascular Territory**:

**Carotid (Anterior Circulation)** — internal carotid / MCA:
• **Contralateral weakness** (face, arm, leg)
• **Contralateral sensory loss**
• **Aphasia** (dominant hemisphere = left side)
• **Neglect** (non-dominant = right side)
• **Amaurosis fugax** (temporary monocular blindness — 'curtain coming down')
• **Homonymous hemianopia** (vision loss on same side in both eyes)

**Vertebrobasilar (Posterior Circulation)** — brainstem, cerebellum, occipital:
• **Dizziness/vertigo** (most common)
• **Diplopia** (double vision)
• **Dysarthria** (slurred speech)
• **Dysphagia** (difficulty swallowing)
• **Ataxia** (coordination problems)
• **Crossed signs** (ipsilateral face + contralateral body = brainstem!)
• **Drop attacks** (sudden collapse without LOC)

**TIA Mimics**: Migraine with aura, seizure, transient hypoglycemia, syncope, anxiety
content_chunks.visual_desc: Brain vascular map: LEFT (carotid/MCA): motor cortex, speech area. RIGHT (vertebrobasilar): brainstem, cerebellum, occipital lobe with corresponding symptoms

content_chunks.title: ABCD² Score: TIA Risk Stratification
content_chunks.content:
**ABCD² Score** — predicts 90-day stroke risk after TIA. **Board favorite!**

**A — Age**: ≥60 = 1 point

**B — BP**: SBP ≥140 or DBP ≥90 = 1 point

**C — Clinical features**:
• Unilateral weakness = **2 points**
• Speech disturbance without weakness = **1 point**
• Other = 0 points

**D — Duration**:
• ≥60 minutes = **2 points**
• 10-59 minutes = **1 point**
• <10 minutes = 0

**D — Diabetes**: Present = 1 point

**Total: 0-7 points**

**Risk Stratification**:
• **Low risk** (0-3): 1% 90-day stroke risk → outpatient workup OK
• **Moderate risk** (4-5): 4% risk → urgent outpatient (within 1 week)
• **High risk** (6-7): 8% risk → **ADMIT** for inpatient workup!

**Regardless of score**: Anyone with crescendo TIA (multiple TIAs in 48h) or TIA with AFib → ADMIT!
content_chunks.clinical_pearl: 🔥 **ABCD² ≥4 = URGENT workup.** Even 'low risk' TIA needs evaluation within 48 hours. The highest stroke risk is in the FIRST 48 hours after TIA, so don't delay! Either admit or arrange urgent carotid imaging + echo.

content_chunks.title: Secondary Prevention: The Stroke Recurrence Busters
content_chunks.content:
**For ALL stroke/TIA patients** (ABCDEFG approach):

**✅ A — Antiplatelet therapy**
• **Non-cardioembolic** (most strokes):
  → **Aspirin 81-325 mg daily** OR
  → **Aspirin + extended-release dipyridamole** (Aggrenox) OR
  → **Clopidogrel 75 mg** daily
  → Recent evidence: **Aspirin + clopidogrel** for 21 days for MINOR stroke/TIA (CHANCE-2 trial)
• **Cardioembolic** (AFib, mechanical valve):
  → **Anticoagulation** (warfarin, apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran)
  → DOACs preferred over warfarin in non-valvular AFib

**✅ B — BP Control**
• Goal <130/80 for most
• Start or intensify antihypertensive 24-48h after ischemic stroke (once stable!)
• Thiazide + ACE-I have best evidence for secondary stroke prevention

**✅ C — Cholesterol management**
• **High-intensity statin** (atorvastatin 40-80 mg or rosuvastatin 20-40 mg)
• LDL goal <70 (or <55 if very high risk)
• Start ASAP — even during hospitalization!

**✅ D — Diabetes control**
• HbA1c <7% (individualize)
• SGLT2i or GLP-1 preferred (CV benefit)

**✅ E — Exercise & lifestyle**
• 150 min/week moderate aerobic activity
• Mediterranean diet (shown to reduce recurrent stroke!)

**✅ F — Follow-up imaging**
• **Carotid duplex**: For anterior circulation TIA/stroke → if stenosis ≥70% → consider **carotid endarterectomy (CEA)** or **stenting (CAS)**
• **Echocardiogram**: TTE + bubble study (to rule out PFO); TEE if high suspicion of cardioembolic source
• **Telemetry/Holter**: Rule out AFib (paroxysmal AFib = the hidden culprit!)

**✅ G — Glucose check**
• Hold metformin for 48h post-contrast if GFR <60

**Lifestyle counseling**:
• **Smoking cessation** (#1 modifiable risk — doubles recurrence risk!)
• **Alcohol moderation** (≤1 drink/day women, ≤2 men)
• **Weight loss if BMI >25**
• **Sleep apnea screening** (treat with CPAP — reduces stroke recurrence!)
content_chunks.visual_desc: 7-pillar diagram: Central 'Stroke Prevention' surrounded by A (aspirin), B (BP target 130/80), C (statin LDL <70), D (diabetes control), E (exercise), F (imaging follow-up), G (GLP-1/SGLT2i if diabetic)

content_chunks.content: 🔥 **Carotid stenosis management**: For **symptomatic** stenosis (TIA or stroke in that carotid territory) ≥70% → **CEA within 2 weeks** of the event! Earlier = better (need a 'cooling off' period of a few days post-stroke). For asymptomatic stenosis ≥60% → medical management with consideration of CEA if life expectancy >5 years.

quick_checks.q: 68-year-old had 20 minutes of right arm weakness and slurred speech yesterday. Now normal. ABCD²: Age=1, BP=0 (128/76), Clinical=2 (weakness), Duration=2, Diabetes=1. Total score: 6. Next step?
a: Start aspirin and see in 1 month
quick_checks.explanation: ABCD² score of **6 = high risk** (8% 90-day stroke risk). This patient needs **ADMISSION** for urgent stroke workup: brain MRI, carotid imaging, echo, telemetry.

quick_checks.q: Which antiplatelet regimen is recommended for a patient with acute minor ischemic stroke?
a: Aspirin + clopidogrel for 21 days, then single agent
quick_checks.explanation: For **minor ischemic stroke** (NIHSS ≤3) or high-risk TIA, **dual antiplatelet therapy (Aspirin + Clopidogrel) for 21 days** then switch to single agent reduces recurrent stroke risk (CHANCE-2/POINT trials).

quick_checks.q: Patient with AFib has TIA. Best choice for secondary prevention?
quick_checks.explanation: **Cardioembolic** strokes from AFib need **ANTICOAGULATION**, not antiplatelets. DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran) are preferred over warfarin for non-valvular AFib.
